text.p: The stability pact designed to control public deficits under European monetary union would ensure there was an appropriate policy mix in the euro currency zone, Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said on Tuesday.

"It was extremely important that in an entity like Europe that we would be sure that the appropriate policy mix would be set up at the level of a single currency area," Trichet told a Paris Europlace conference.

"There you have the explanation for Maastricht treaty provisions as regards fiscal policy for the stability and growth pact. You also have the explanation for the declaration on co-ordination of economic policy."

He said this combination of the stability pact, ratified at a recent Amsterdam summit, and an agreement among member states to coordinate economic policy closely answered U.S. concerns that the single currency would not function properly without a federal budget system.
"We are in a very special entity in Europe. There is no federal budget, there is no automatic setting up of the appropriate policy mix," he said.
"We are in a universe where only very close co-ordination among various international governments can deliver, at the level of the euro zone, the equivalent of a federal government in Europe.

"The paradox in Europe is that the council, that is the meeting of the governments concerned, has more power on the various domestic fiscal policies, for example, than the U.S. government (has) on Texas, California or Massachusetts.
"This is precisely because the equivalent of the (U.S.) federal government is the addition of the (European) national budgets," Trichet added.
